newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen, from peasant to premier.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen, from peasant to premier.

text.p: Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, the bright son of a peasant family, rose to be Cambodia's strongman through a combination of craft, chance and strategy.
His uneasy truce with First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh broke down last week as their troops clashed after Hun Sen's men attempted to disarm forces under Ranariddh's command.
Ranariddh accused Hun Sen of attempting a coup but a radio station controlled by Hun Sen denied on Sunday that a coup was under way.
Hun Sen had accused Ranariddh of illegally negotiating with the Khmer Rouge and of bringing Khmer Rouge troops into the capital. Ranariddh has denied the charge.

After a meteoric rise from total obscurity in the late 1970s to become the world's youngest prime minister in 1985, Hun Sen was seen as the acceptable face of Cambodian communism through subsequent peace negotiations and U.N.-run elections in 1993.

After the polls he emerged as the leading figure in the Cambodian People's Party (CPP), step by step rolling back the defences of the royalist FUNCINPEC party, which had won the elections, and asserting a leadership that brooks no criticism.

Critics see him as an unpredictable autocrat, overreacting to reasonable demands of his coalition partners and ignoring the rights of the loyal opposition. Others laud him as a master politician and the firm, tough leader the country needs.

He briefly patched up rocky ties with FUNCINPEC's Prince Norodom Ranariddh to engineer a major split within the Khmer Rouge -- the coalition's major achievement, with thousands of guerrillas joining the government since August 1996.

But the ill-feeling, focusing on the issue of power-sharing, returned with each co-premier trying to woo Khmer Rouge defectors over to his side ahead of next May's general election when the allegiance of defectors is expected to be a major factor.

The self-assured politician and fiery orator whose post of second prime minister belies his real position in the power equation seems a world removed from the skinny, awkward and media-shy 33-year-old who took over as premier in January 1985.
The raw material was there, however, as journalist Elizabeth Becker noted of her first meeting with Hun Sen in the mid-1980s.
"Even then it was quite clear he was the brains," she said, adding that although he came out with communist jargon, "he was very intelligent -- he could take an argument, dissect it."
That Hun Sen ever reached the premier's office owes much to fate -- the civil war of the early 1970s, his defection from the Khmer Rouge and the Vietnamese invasion of Cambodia in 1978.
Hun Sen was born of a farming family on April 4, 1951 in the eastern province of Kompong Cham.

He joined forces led by the Khmer Rouge during their 1970-75 guerrilla war against the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government that ousted head of state Prince (later King) Norodom Sihanouk in 1970. Operating in the eastern part of the country, he rose to command a brigade.
The Khmer Rouge seized power on April 17, 1975, driving almost the entire population into work camps in an agrarian revolution that left more than a million people dead.

Hun Sen, who lost an eye in the last days of the war, claims he was never a Khmer Rouge officer but went underground in 1970 to help Sihanouk fight Lon Nol and the "American aggressors." He said he defected to Vietnam in June 1977.
Hanoi installed Hun Sen and other defectors as leaders of the People's Republic of Kampuchea in 1979, with Hun Sen as foreign minister of a government shunned by much of the world.
He became premier in 1985 and led talks with the U.N.-recognised three-party guerrilla front, headed by Sihanouk but dominated by the Khmer Rouge.
The western world came to view him as a moderate with whom it could do business and Hun Sen cultivated the image of being open to democratic ideas up to U.N.-run elections in 1993.
The polls produced a pact between the four parties that won seats but only after Hun Sen's renamed Cambodian People's Party raised the spectre of renewed war if FUNCINPEC did not agree.

He began to pay lip service to the democratic ideals enshrined in the new constitution, while chipping away with increasing confidence at the already limited power of his royalist partners and ignoring the rights of opponents.
When Ranariddh threatened to quit the coalition unless his party got more power, a confident Hun Sen responded with threats of force to rein in his rival.
